claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaims 1–3 concerning whether safety-relevant representations are eliminated or bypassed, run paired forward passes on open-weight safety-aligned models such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, and Gemma-2-9B-it using harmful prompts from HarmBench, AdvBench, and JailbreakBench. For each harmful request, retain the plain version and one or more jailbreak variants that are verified to change refusal into substantive compliance by the HarmBench evaluator plus a blinded human audit; include benign prompts matched for topic, vocabulary, and jailbreak-template style. Record residual-stream states and individual attention-head outputs at every layer and token. Train diagnostic probes only on plain harmful versus benign prompts, freeze them, and test cross-condition decoding on successful jailbreaks; also measure representational similarity and harmfulness-direction projections between plain and jailbroken versions. Above-chance, well-calibrated cross-decoding across models and unseen attack families would show that harmfulness information persists, favoring bypass over elimination; collapse to benign-level decoding throughout the network would support elimination, while persistence only in early layers would weaken the broad claim. Public release of equivalent paired activations and preregistered cross-attack analyses could make rerunning this experiment unnecessary.

To address subclaim 4, that a jailbreak selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, use the successful paired cases from Experiment 1 to quantify, for every head, changes in output norm, attention pattern, and projection onto the clean harmfulness/refusal direction at matched semantic token positions. Fit a hierarchical model across prompts, attacks, layers, and model families, with false-discovery control, and compare the concentration of suppression with random-head, benign-template, prompt-length, and token-position controls. Define 'small' prospectively, for example as at most 1% of all heads explaining at least 50% of the attack-associated reduction in the refusal-direction signal, and test whether the same heads recur across held-out prompts and attack families. Concentrated, reproducible suppression specific to successful attacks would support the subclaim; diffuse changes, inconsistent head identities, or equally strong suppression on benign template controls would refute or substantially qualify it. Published head-level causal or activation data covering the same models and controls could obviate this experiment.

To address subclaim 5, that suppressing the identified small subset of heads is by itself sufficient to turn refusal into compliance, causally intervene on plain harmful prompts from held-out HarmBench, AdvBench, and JailbreakBench splits. Zero, scale down, or replace only the candidate heads' safety-direction components with their values from matched successful-jailbreak runs while leaving all other activations unchanged; score substantive compliance using the HarmBench evaluator and blinded human review. Compare against equal-size random head sets, heads matched by activation norm or layer, full-head versus direction-only ablation, and interventions on benign tasks from MMLU and AlpacaEval to detect generic model damage. Test necessity as a complementary intervention by restoring the clean-prompt safety component in those heads during successful jailbreaks. A large and reproducible refusal-to-compliance shift from candidate-head suppression, together with restored refusal under reverse patching and little benign degradation, would establish sufficiency and support bypass; no shift, effects requiring many heads, or nonspecific incoherence would reject the strong causal claim. Existing public intervention results with code, exact head sets, and random-head controls could make this test unnecessary.

To address subclaim 6, that other attention heads continue representing harmful content during successful jailbreaks, remove the causally implicated subset from all analyses and test each remaining head and prespecified layer-wise aggregates for harmfulness information. Train linear probes on plain HarmBench or AdvBench harmful prompts versus topic- and style-matched benign examples, freeze all weights and thresholds, and evaluate only on successful jailbreaks from unseen JailbreakBench attack families; use label permutation, minimum-description-length probing, low-rank controls, and lexical adversarial examples to ensure that decoding is not due merely to keywords or probe capacity. Also patch the harmfulness-direction component from these remaining heads into benign matched prompts to distinguish decodable information from causal control of refusal. Robust decoding from many nonimplicated heads, despite their inability to restore refusal individually, would show that harmful content remains represented while the behavior-control pathway is bypassed; disappearance of decodability after removing the suppressed subset would contradict the claim. A sufficiently broad public head-wise decoding study on successful, behavior-verified jailbreaks could replace this experiment.

To address subclaims 7 and 8, concerning direct harmful-input detection without additional training, preregister a genuinely zero-training readout before examining detector labels. For example, at a fixed layer chosen independently of safety data, score the residual stream or noncausal-head aggregate by its cosine projection onto the model's own unembedding-vector contrast for fixed words such as 'harmful' minus 'harmless', use zero as the fixed threshold, and fit no probe, head weights, or threshold. Separately report a weaker 'no gradient training' variant that uses the head subset discovered in Experiments 2–4 and a benign-only quantile threshold, clearly labeling this as calibrated rather than strictly training-free. Evaluate both on held-out HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, and benign WildChat or LMSYS-Chat-1M examples, including unseen jailbreak families, multilingual items where available, and topic-matched benign controls. Strong AUROC and useful fixed-threshold sensitivity and specificity for the strict rule would support direct zero-training readout; success only after supervised head selection, label-based thresholding, or probe fitting would refute the 'no additional training' wording while possibly supporting a weaker low-training claim. A fully specified, frozen readout released before evaluation on these datasets could make this experiment largely unnecessary.

To address subclaim 9, that the representation-based detector is competitive with dedicated safety models, benchmark the frozen detector from Experiment 5 against public dedicated safeguards such as Llama Guard 3, ShieldGemma, and the HarmBench classifier on identical, contamination-audited test sets from HarmBench, JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT, WildChat or LMSYS-Chat-1M, and multilingual safety datasets available on Hugging Face. Report AUROC, AUPRC under realistic class imbalance, recall at 1% and 5% false-positive rates, expected calibration error, per-category and per-attack-family performance, bootstrap confidence intervals, latency, memory, and whether access to the generator's internal activations gives an operational cost advantage. Freeze every method before testing and include cross-model transfer, testing whether a readout identified in one generator works in another, as a stringent robustness check. Statistically noninferior safety performance across unseen attacks and categories, with comparable false-positive rates and lower incremental cost, would justify 'competitive'; superiority only on the same model or attacks used to identify heads would indicate overfitting, and materially worse low-FPR recall would reject the claim. Public, independently reproduced head-to-head evaluations using the same frozen splits and metrics could obviate this final benchmark.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Layer- and component-resolved comparison on behaviorally paired clean and successful-attack inputs that can distinguish preservation of a safety-relevant signal from network-wide erasure.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed paired passes record residual-stream and head states throughout the network, freeze diagnostics trained on clean harmful-versus-benign data, and test decoding, similarity, and direction projections on successful jailbreaks. Those measurements would reveal whether safety-relevant harmfulness information remains detectable or collapses to benign levels, even though the readout is not implemented with exactly the same direction statistic.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A behavior-verified, within-prompt paired corpus containing refused harmful requests and substantively successful variants across diverse attack procedures, large enough to support the downstream comparisons.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 explicitly retains plain harmful requests and jailbreak variants only after evaluator and human verification of refusal-to-compliance changes, with multiple attack sources and matched benign controls. Proposed 1 and the held-out intervention and decoding designs extend the paired cases across prompts and unseen attack families. The claim does not bind the particular source datasets or the reference study's exact yield.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A component-level scoring and classification procedure that identifies concentrated suppressing and persistent head populations, with controls and robustness checks showing that the identification is not an arbitrary threshold artifact.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 1 measures every head's output, attention, and safety-direction changes, models variation across prompts and layers, controls false discoveries and confounds, defines concentration prospectively, and tests recurrence on held-out attacks. Proposed 2 uses the resulting candidates for causal testing and proposed 3 separately analyzes the remaining heads. This supplies comparable head identification and validation without requiring the reference's particular density-estimation procedure or cutoff sweep.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A controlled causal intervention on the candidate heads with a refusal-to-compliance behavioral endpoint, nonspecific equal-size intervention controls, and enough replication or uncertainty analysis to attribute the effect to those heads.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 2 intervenes only on candidate heads in held-out harmful cases, measures substantive compliance, compares equal-size random and matched controls, tests several intervention forms, includes benign-task damage checks, and attempts reverse patching during successful attacks. These outcomes would establish whether the small candidate set is sufficient rather than merely correlated with jailbreak success.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence from successful attacks that heads outside the causally implicated subset still encode harmful-content information or contribute to a persistent mid-network signal.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 3 removes the implicated subset from the analysis and evaluates frozen probes on each remaining head and layer aggregate using successful attacks from unseen families, with lexical and capacity controls. The additional patching analysis distinguishes information that remains decodable from information that directly controls refusal. Proposed 0 independently supplies all-layer and all-head cross-condition persistence measurements.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-level attribution that separates the heads' response to the original harmful request from their response to the jailbreak template, showing whether the head-type difference is attack-template-specific rather than a generic difference in harmful-content sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set compares matched semantic positions, template controls, attention patterns, and lexical adversarial examples, so it gets at whether suppression is attack-specific. However, it never explicitly decomposes each head's activation into contributions from original-request tokens versus attack-template tokens. A changed output or decoding pattern could therefore still reflect an unresolved interaction between harmful-content sensitivity and the template, rather than the specific token-source dissociation established by the reference.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment separates original harmful-request contributions from attack-template contributions and uses their contrast to rule out generic harmful-content sensitivity as the explanation for the two head types.

[2] Proposed 0 records token-position states and proposed 1 adds matched-position and benign-template controls, but neither specifies an input-token contribution decomposition for the two head populations.

[3] Those measurements can show attack-associated and localized changes without determining whether the head-type difference comes from the template tokens or from sensitivity to the harmful request itself.
[4] A team running the proposed set would therefore fail to learn the reference experiment's precise mechanistic dissociation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An externally evaluated, genuinely training-free activation readout tested across varied models, safety tasks, attack families, and benign data, with direct comparison against the model's behavior and dedicated safety systems using comparable operating-point metrics.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 4 preregisters a strict zero-training readout with a fixed layer, fixed projection, and fixed threshold, and evaluates it on held-out harmful, jailbreak, benign, multilingual, and unseen-attack data. Proposed 5 benchmarks that frozen readout against dedicated safeguards on shared contamination-audited sets, reporting discrimination, calibration, low-false-positive recall, category and attack-family breakdowns, uncertainty, and cross-model transfer. The proposed scope is different but provides the external generalization and competitiveness evidence required by the claim.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would directly test persistence versus erasure, identify concentrated head changes, establish causal sufficiency with nonspecific controls, test representation in the remaining heads, and evaluate a strictly training-free detector against dedicated safeguards. Its main unresolved issue is the mechanistic rival addressed by reference experiment 5: the set does not separate original harmful-request token contributions from jailbreak-template token contributions. Thus it would largely settle the stated claim, but the strongest attack-template-specific bypass interpretation would remain incompletely discriminated.
missing: An explicit token-level attribution or equivalent intervention that compares the two head populations on original harmful-request tokens separately from jailbreak-template tokens, ruling out generic harmful-content sensitivity as the source of their difference.
missing_all_runs: A source-resolved token contribution analysis comparing the selected and remaining head groups on original harmful-request tokens versus attack-template tokens, ideally with a prespecified criterion for similarity on the former and divergence on the latter.

An explicit token-level attention-contribution analysis comparing the candidate suppressed heads and remaining heads on original harmful-request tokens versus jailbreak-template tokens, with controls for contextual and positional effects.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A behavior-verified paired corpus in which the same harmful request is refused in its plain form and substantively complied with after attack, with enough attack and prompt diversity for within-pair inference.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 0 constructs plain/jailbroken pairs and verifies the refusal-to-compliance transition with an evaluator and blinded human audit, while sampling multiple harmful-prompt sources, attack families, matched benign controls, and unseen attacks. reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible component-level scoring and classification procedure that identifies concentrated attack-related changes, controls arbitrary cut points and confounds, and tests whether the identified component groups are stable.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 1 scores every head using several activation measures and the clean safety direction, models variation across prompts and attacks, controls random heads and positional/template confounds, applies false-discovery control, and tests recurrence on held-out prompts and attack families. Its prospective concentration rule and hierarchical validation provide an alternative calibration to a threshold-and-bandwidth sweep.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A controlled causal intervention showing whether suppressing the identified small component subset changes refusal into substantive compliance, relative to equally sized controls and with evidence that the effect is not generic damage.

These controls can establish sufficiency and distinguish it from nonspecific perturbation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that non-suppressed heads retain a measurable harmful-content signal during successful attacks, rather than the persistent signal being confined to the selectively suppressed group.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 3 removes the implicated subset from the analysis and tests the remaining heads and layer aggregates with frozen cross-condition decoders on successful, unseen jailbreaks. Robust decoding from those remaining components, supplemented by patching controls, would directly establish that harmful-content information persists outside the suppressed group.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-level attribution that separates each head group's contribution from the original harmful request from its contribution from the attack template, allowing a template-specific mechanism to be distinguished from merely different harmful-content sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set records token-resolved head outputs, compares head-level attack effects with template and positional controls, and uses lexical adversarial controls. However, it does not explicitly decompose each head's activation into contributions from original harmful-request tokens versus attack-template tokens and compare the two head groups on those separate contributions.
reasoning_chain: [1] Reference experiment 5 distinguishes the bypass mechanism from the rival explanation of generic differential sensitivity by attributing head activity to request tokens and attack-template tokens separately.
[2] Proposed experiments 0, 1, and 3 provide token-resolved measurements and several template, position, and lexical controls, so they get at that distinction.

[3] Without an explicit per-token contribution decomposition and head-group comparison on the two token sources, a head effect could still reflect contextual or harmful-content sensitivity rather than template-specific routing.
[4] A team running the proposed set would therefore fail to learn the specific mechanistic separation established by reference experiment 5: partial.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A training-free harmful-input readout tested for transfer across diverse models and safety tasks, with quantitative comparison against the model's own behavior and dedicated safety baselines.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed 4 preregisters and evaluates a genuinely zero-training fixed readout, while separately labeling weaker calibrated variants, across held-out harmful/benign data and unseen attack families. Proposed 5 benchmarks the frozen detector against dedicated safeguards using contamination-audited common splits, low-false-positive metrics, calibration, uncertainty, category and attack-family breakdowns, and cross-model transfer. Together these test direct usability, no-additional-training status, generalization, and competitiveness.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly covers the claim's main empirical components: persistence versus elimination, selective head suppression, causal refusal-to-compliance conversion, persistence in other heads, zero-training readout, and comparison with dedicated safeguards. It leaves one meaningful mechanistic ambiguity: the proposed analyses do not explicitly separate the two head groups' contributions to original harmful-request tokens from their contributions to jailbreak-template tokens. Thus the behavioral and representational claim could be substantially evaluated, but the more specific template-routing account supported by the reference set would not be fully settled.
missing: An explicit token-level attention-contribution analysis comparing the candidate suppressed heads and remaining heads on original harmful-request tokens versus jailbreak-template tokens, with controls for contextual and positional effects.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A direct, layer- and component-resolved comparison of safety-relevant activation between matched successful attacks and unattacked refusals, capable of distinguishing persistence from network-wide erasure.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 records residual-stream and head states throughout the network, compares plain and successful jailbreak versions, and tests frozen cross-condition decoding and direction projections. Persistence or collapse is explicitly used as the decision criterion, so the team would learn whether the relevant information survives the attack.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A sufficiently large, behavior-verified paired set in which the same harmful request is observed in refused and successful-compliance conditions, enabling attack effects to be separated from request-content effects.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 constructs plain/jailbreak pairs and verifies the behavioral change with automated evaluation and human review, while the later experiments use held-out successful cases, matched controls, and multiple attack sources. This supplies the within-request contrast needed by the reference analysis.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A calibrated component-level scoring and classification procedure that identifies attack-associated and persistent head groups and demonstrates that the classification is robust to analytic choices and controls.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 scores every head using several activation-related measures, uses prespecified concentration criteria, false-discovery control, random and benign-template controls, and held-out recurrence tests. Experiments 2 and 3 then use the identified and remaining groups causally and representationally, providing a comparable validation of the component classification without requiring the same statistic or cutoff procedure.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal intervention showing that perturbing only the selected small head subset changes a normally refused harmful request into substantive compliance, with matched perturbation controls and evidence that the effect is not generic damage.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 1 identifies the candidate subset, and proposed experiment 2 intervenes only on those heads or their safety-direction components, compares equal-size random and matched controls, measures substantive compliance, and tests reverse restoration and benign-task effects. The resulting outcomes would establish or reject sufficiency and specificity.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that heads outside the attack-suppressed subset retain harmful-content information during verified successful jailbreaks, rather than merely reflecting a change in the refusal behavior.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 3 removes the implicated subset and evaluates frozen decoding from the remaining heads on unseen successful attacks, with lexical and capacity controls. Its additional patching analysis distinguishes retained decodable harmful information from mere behavior-level correlation, so it bears directly on persistence in the other heads.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A token- or source-resolved comparison showing that the two head groups treat the original harmful request similarly but diverge specifically on attack-template content, thereby separating bypass specialization from a simple difference in harmful-content sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed set compares matched plain and jailbroken inputs, head-level changes, attention patterns, token positions, template controls, and lexical adversaries. Those analyses can show attack-associated differences, but they do not explicitly decompose each head's activation into contributions from the original harmful-request tokens versus attack-template tokens. A sensitivity difference tied to changed context or token composition would therefore remain a live explanation.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment distinguishes the bypass account from the rival claim that the head groups merely have different sensitivity to harmful content by isolating request-token and attack-template contributions.
[2] Proposed experiments 0, 1, and 3 provide matched inputs, token-position and template controls, and lexical checks, but no source-resolved contribution analysis for the two token sets.

[3] An observed difference between candidate and remaining heads could consequently still arise from different sensitivity to harmful content or altered contextual composition rather than selective response to the attack template.
[4] The team would not conclusively learn the reference experiment's mechanistic distinction between template-specific specialization and generic harmful-content sensitivity.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An externally evaluated, genuinely training-free harmful-input readout whose transfer and detection quality are measured across models, attack conditions, safety domains, and dedicated safety baselines.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 4 preregisters a frozen zero-training readout with a fixed rule and evaluates it on held-out harmful, benign, and unseen-jailbreak data. Proposed experiment 5 benchmarks that frozen detector against dedicated safeguards using multiple discrimination, calibration, subgroup, transfer, and cost metrics. Together they establish whether persistent representations are directly usable and competitively effective.

The remaining evidential gap is mechanistic: the set does not cleanly separate contributions from the original harmful request and the attack template, so it cannot fully rule out a generic head-sensitivity explanation for the observed specialization.
